Clinical: Regular assessment for symptom resolution and adverse drug reactions.
Drug-related: Severe adverse drug reactions, drug-resistant TB.
Adverse Drug Reactions: Vigilantly monitor for side effects of antifungal and antiparasitic agents.
Identify the primary pharmacological problem – e.g., drug‑induced hepatotoxicity, therapeutic failure, adverse drug reaction, or drug‑drug interaction.
Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) – ranging from mild GI upset to life‑threatening Stevens‑Johnson syndrome; early detection improves outcome.
Polypharmacy complications – adverse drug reactions, drug‑drug interactions, medication non‑adherence.
Adverse drug reaction (ADR) – any noxious, unintended response to a medication at doses normally used for prophylaxis, diagnosis or therapy.

qs.q: Besides being used as a mucolytic and antidote for acetaminophen overdose, N-Acetylcysteine has which notable adverse drug reaction?
qs.e: N-Acetylcysteine can cause bronchospasm, along with stomatitis, rhinorrhea, and rash. It does not typically cause urinary retention or extrapyramidal symptoms, which are profile features of anticholinergics and first-generation antipsychotics respectively.

faq.a: Look for a clear temporal link, improvement after stopping the drug, and lack of an alternative diagnosis.
faq.q: How do I decide if a reaction is drug‑related or disease‑related?

faq.a: The Hartwig level system, because it relies on clinical actions (e.g., need for ICU) rather than extensive labs.
faq.q: What is the most practical severity scale in a low‑resource ward?

faq.a: For severe reactions like SJS/TEN, short‑course systemic steroids are acceptable when no alternative is available, but stop the offending drug first.
faq.q: Can I give steroids for a drug rash if I lack a dermatologist?

exam: A patient on isoniazid develops jaundice after 6 weeks – what is your next step and why? — Assess LFTs, stop isoniazid, consider alternative TB regimen; early withdrawal prevents severe hepatotoxicity.
You suspect an ADR but the drug level test is unavailable – how do you confirm causality? — Use temporal relationship, de‑challenge, and rule out other causes; apply the Naranjo algorithm if needed.

A child on quinine for severe malaria becomes hypoglycaemic – which mechanism explains this and what immediate action is required? — Quinidine stimulates insulin release; give IV glucose promptly and monitor blood sugar.

During ward round you note a new maculopapular rash in a patient on cotrimoxazole; what questions help differentiate ADR from viral exanthem? — Ask onset relative to drug start, presence of fever, other drug exposures, and whether rash improves after stopping cotrimoxazole.

A patient on gentamicin shows rising creatinine; how do you stage severity and decide on drug continuation? — Use Hartwig level 3 (moderate); stop gentamicin, switch to less nephrotoxic agent, monitor renal function.

Explain why polypharmacy increases ADR risk in HIV/TB co‑infection and list two preventive measures. — Overlapping metabolism (e.g., rifampicin induces CYP450) raises toxic levels; use fixed‑dose combos, review meds weekly.
What red‑flag sign distinguishes anaphylaxis from a simple urticarial drug reaction? — Rapid onset of airway swelling, hypotension, or bronchospasm indicates anaphylaxis.
A patient on warfarin develops a sudden INR of 6 without dose change – what ADR should you suspect and how manage it? — Warfarin over‑anticoagulation; give vitamin K, hold warfarin, monitor INR.
ai.title: Adverse Drug Reactions
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are harmful, unintended responses to medicines at normal doses. Recognising patterns, severity and causality guides urgent care and long‑term prevention, especially where diagnostics are limited.

b: Temporal link: symptoms start after drug exposure
Improvement after stopping the drug (de‑challenge)
Re‑appearance if drug is re‑started (re‑challenge, if safe)
No alternative disease explanation
sections.p: An ADR is any noxious, unintended response to a drug taken at therapeutic doses. Diagnosis rests on temporal relationship, de‑challenge/re‑challenge, and exclusion of other causes.

b: Mild (Level 1‑2): requires no change or only drug withdrawal
Moderate (Level 3‑4): needs treatment or prolongs hospital stay
Severe (Level 5‑7): life‑threatening, causes permanent damage or death
sections.p: The WHO‑Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC) classification and the Hartwig severity scale are commonly used.

b: Type A: dose‑related, e.g., aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity, quinine‑induced hypoglycaemia
Type B: idiosyncratic, e.g., sulfonamide rash, Stevens‑Johnson syndrome from sulfa drugs
Polypharmacy: drug‑drug interactions common with antiretrovirals, anti‑TB drugs, antimalarials
Herbal/traditional medicines: may potentiate hepatotoxicity (e.g., kava, herbal teas)
sections.p: ADRs arise from predictable (type A) pharmacologic effects or unpredictable (type B) immune‑mediated reactions.

b: Gastro‑intestinal: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea (e.g., metronidazole, antimalarials)
Cutaneous: maculopapular rash, urticaria, SJS/TEN (sulfonamides, antiretrovirals)
Hepatic: jaundice, raised transaminases (isoniazid, antituberculars)
Renal: reduced urine output, rising creatinine (aminoglycosides, tenofovir)
Haematologic: thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis (chloramphenicol, carbamazepine)
sections.p: Presentation varies by organ system and drug class; common patterns in low‑resource settings include GI upset, rash, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and haemorrhage.
Targeted tests answer specific questions about organ injury and causality.

t.b: Is there haematologic toxicity? – Low neutrophils suggest agranulocytosis; low platelets suggest drug‑induced thrombocytopenia
Is there hepatotoxicity? – ALT >5 × ULN or bilirubin >2 mg/dL signals significant injury
Is there renal impairment? – Creatinine rise >0.5 mg/dL or eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates nephrotoxicity
Is the drug concentration toxic? – Levels above therapeutic range predict toxicity
Confirms immune‑mediated epidermal necrosis – guides prognosis

b: Stevens‑Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis – extensive skin loss, mucosal involvement
Anaphylaxis – airway compromise, hypotension
Severe hepatotoxicity – INR >1.5, encephalopathy
Acute kidney injury – oliguria, rising creatinine
Drug‑induced arrhythmia (e.g., QT prolongation) – syncope, torsades
sections.p: Certain ADRs demand immediate action to prevent death or permanent damage.

b: Immediate drug withdrawal; document the reaction
Supportive care: IV fluids for nephrotoxicity, antihistamines for rash, corticosteroids for severe SJS/TEN (if available)
Specific antidotes: N‑acetylcysteine for acetaminophen, vitamin K for warfarin over‑anticoagulation
Avoid cross‑reactive drugs (e.g., avoid all sulfonamides after sulfa rash)
Report ADR to national pharmacovigilance centre
sections.p: First stop the suspected drug, then treat organ injury and prevent recurrence.

b: Create a medication list with allergy/ADR tags
Use WHO‑essential medicines list to limit unnecessary drugs
Educate patients on early warning signs
Screen for high‑risk groups: HIV on antiretrovirals, TB on rifampicin, malaria on artemisinin combos
Regularly review drug regimens during ward rounds
sections.p: Long‑term strategies reduce future ADRs, especially in polypharmacy environments.

b: Drug‑induced liver injury vs viral hepatitis – viral serology helps
Nephrotoxicity vs dehydration – assess volume status and urine output
Allergic rash vs viral exanthem – timing relative to drug start is key
sections.p: Distinguish ADRs from disease progression, infection, or drug‑withdrawal syndromes.

b: Normal ALT early in acetaminophen toxicity – rely on timing and dose history
Elevated bilirubin from hemolysis mimicking hepatotoxicity – check haptoglobin, LDH
Creatinine rise due to muscle wasting in HIV – interpret with cystatin C if available
sections.p: Laboratory values may be normal early or altered by other conditions.
